content: The process of obtaining ethical approval, conducting training, and piloting the study is essential before initiating data collection. Data collection occurs at the facility level and, if necessary, at the community level. It also includes data collection at levels above the facility. Post-data collection activities involve data analysis, preparation of reports and papers, creation of a publicly accessible database, and dissemination of the data. The guidelines are divided into four sections: Section B: Defining the Tuberculosis (TB) Interventions to Be Costed This section provides an overview of TB interventions, with additional details available in Appendix 2. It emphasizes the importance of developing standardized unit costs for TB services to enable cross-country comparisons and extrapolation of costs across different settings. The main categories of TB interventions include vaccination (e.g., Bacille Calmette-Guérin or BCG vaccination), TB case detection and diagnosis (including passive, active, and intensified case finding), TB treatment, TB prevention, TB infection control, and above-site TB program services (e.g., policy, planning, coordination, and management). Future technologies and interventions, such as new vaccine candidates, may also be included. For each intervention, standardized unit costs are presented to ensure comparability and generalizability. These costs are broken down into direct and ancillary costs, with further breakdowns into activity costs determined by the quantity of inputs multiplied by their price. Section C: Study Design and Setup This section focuses on the design and setup of a TB costing study, highlighting key steps in the process. It includes pre-data collection activities such as conceptualizing the study, forming the core research team, planning meetings to define objectives and responsibilities, identifying funding sources, and establishing links with relevant countries or partners. Ethical approval processes, training of research staff, and piloting of data collection tools are also covered. The study protocol must be developed and submitted for ethical approval, and a technical advisory group should be established to assist with decision-making and strategic direction. Section D: Data Collection This section outlines the features of data collection, including resource and service use measurement, pricing, and valuation. It details the costing approaches and introduces the Value TB Costing Tool Suite. Key aspects include the scope, methods, sampling, data sources, timing of data collection, and adjustments to data. The section emphasizes the importance of accurately capturing all inputs and outputs required for TB interventions to ensure unbiased cost estimates. Section E: Data Analysis, Presentation of Results, and Dissemination of Cost Data This section addresses the analysis of unit costs generated during the study. It highlights the need to examine cost drivers, variations in costs, and conduct sensitivity analyses to assess uncertainty. The results should be disseminated transparently and effectively to users of TB unit costs. Appendix 11 provides case studies to illustrate practical steps for costing TB services. Appendices and Additional Details Appendix 3 outlines the main TB intervention categories, intervention details, and standardized cost units to be reported. It includes examples of unit costs for various TB interventions, such as the cost per treatment month for drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB) and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), cost per outpatient visit, cost per inpatient bed-day, and cost per diagnostic test. The costing process involves understanding and describing the production process for each intervention, building up the cost from different components, and ensuring the cost is not biased. This requires collaboration with TB service planners and detailed descriptions of inputs and outputs. Study Objectives and Setup The study begins with identifying the need for primary costing based on the intended use of cost estimates and the availability of existing cost data. If existing data are detailed, recent, and of sufficient quality, primary costing may not be necessary. The purpose of the costing study must be clearly defined, and the study team should be established. Planning meetings should define TB costing needs, develop study questions, and assign roles and responsibilities. Sampling of high TB burden countries and inclusion of study partners, such as national TB programs and local research groups, should be considered. Ethical approval processes and training of research staff are critical steps before data collection begins. Training and Piloting Once ethical approval is obtained, a study pilot can be conducted alongside initial training. This process, which typically takes around two months, helps refine generic tools (e.g., the Value TB Costing Tool Suite) and directs data collection efforts.
